question: The end of 2023 marked six years since pollution control rules for large combustion plants came into force under the Energy Community Treaty. However, a new report1 shows that last year, sulphur dioxide emissions from coal plants included in the national emission reduction plans of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo, North Macedonia and Serbia were still collectively 5.7 times higher than allowed.

Dust and nitrogen oxide emissions also remained above the legal limits. Clearly, pollution control investments are either not happening, or are not producing results. In addition, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro and Serbia are now also violating the ‘opt-out’, or limited lifetime derogation, by failing to close plants after their permitted operating hours have been reached.

Despite these persistent breaches, none of the Western Balkan coal power plant operators has been fined by the national environmental authorities. The EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism will weaken the region’s coal industry, but this will take several years. People’s health cannot wait: immediate action is needed. What action is the Commission taking: 1.
to make it clear to the Western Balkan governments that countries participating in the EU energy market must enforce pollution control legislation?
to include effective, dissuasive and proportionate penalties for non-compliance in the Energy Community Treaty?
by CEE Bankwatch Network.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (16.1.2025) The Commission is aware of the CEE Bankwatch Network report mentioned by the Honourable Members. 1. All the five countries concerned by the report have the status of EU candidate or potential candidate and are therefore expected to gradually align with the EU environmental acquis, including in the sectors of air quality and industrial pollution control.

Considering that EU legislation is not binding for the five countries before their accession to the EU, infringement procedures cannot be initiated. However, their compliance with the relevant EU acquis is evaluated as part of their progress assessment.

The Commission attaches great importance to environmental issues in the context of the accession negotiations and will continue to raise1 with the authorities of the five concerned countries the proper alignment with EU air quality and industrial pollution control acquis, including in the framework of the Stabilisation and Association Agreements2 concluded between the EU and those countries. 2.

The Western Balkan countries are also Contracting Parties of the Energy Community Treaty3 and bound by its rules, including as regards emissions and decarbonisation. The Energy Community Secretariat assists these countries in the implementation of these rules. Non-compliance is followed up by means of dispute settlement procedures which are usually launched by the Energy Community Secretariat.

The region is also bound by the 2030 Climate and Energy targets4, and the obligation to adopt and update National Energy and Climate Plans5, using the same template as EU Member States, setting out their actions to reach the targets, including gradual phasing out of coal from electricity production.
